doctrines/humanity-sin/question: What does it mean to be made in God’s image — and how deep does sin go?
doctrines/humanity-sin/summary: Christians agree that humans are created in God’s image and that all have sinned, but differ on what the image is, how body, soul and spirit relate, where souls come from, whether Adam’s guilt or only his mortality is inherited, and whether fallen humans can freely turn to God.
doctrines/humanity-sin/longText:
Genesis says that God made humankind “in our image, after our likeness … male and female”, and formed the man from dust and breathed life into him. Early Christian writers read this richly: Irenaeus distinguished the image from the likeness and pictured humanity created young, to grow; Gregory of Nyssa located the image in freedom and in humanity as a whole; Augustine found a trinitarian image in memory, understanding and will; Aquinas located it in the rational mind. In the 20th century Karl Barth and others proposed a relational reading, and Old Testament scholars a royal-functional one — humans as God’s representatives and stewards. Debates over the parts of a human being run alongside: most churches teach body and soul (the Council of Vienne, 1312, called the soul the form of the body), trichotomists such as Watchman Nee distinguish spirit from soul, and Christian physicalists today argue for a wholly embodied person awaiting resurrection. Whether souls are transmitted from parents (Tertullian’s traducianism), created individually by God (Jerome, Aquinas, Catholic teaching) or pre-exist (Origen, condemned in 553) has never been settled outside Catholicism.

The doctrine of original sin divides East and West. Greek and Syriac Fathers such as Chrysostom taught that Adam’s descendants inherit death and a wounded nature; Augustine, in controversy with Pelagius, taught that all sinned in Adam and inherit both guilt and corruption, a view confirmed at Carthage (418) and Orange (529) and by Trent and the Protestant confessions. Reformed covenant theology framed Adam as federal head whose guilt is imputed; Zwingli described original sin as a disease rather than guilt; Jonathan Edwards defended original sin by arguing that God constitutes humanity one with Adam. In the 20th century Orthodox theologians such as John Romanides made “ancestral sin” a point of sharp contrast with Augustine.

The Reformation turned the question into one of freedom: against Erasmus, Luther argued for the bondage of the will; Calvinists confessed total depravity; Arminians and Wesleyans answered with a universal prevenient grace. Philosophers continue to debate libertarian and compatibilist accounts of freedom.

Finally, Christian anthropology has an uncomfortable history. The same tradition that proclaimed the dignity of every image-bearer also produced Tertullian’s “devil’s gateway”, Aquinas’ Aristotelian description of woman as “misbegotten”, the conquest of the Americas and theological defences of racial slavery and apartheid. At Valladolid (1550) Las Casas argued for the full humanity and rights of Indigenous peoples; abolitionists, Black and feminist theologians and the churches that condemned apartheid as heresy drew on the image of God and the doctrine of sin to expose these hierarchies. Recent genomic evidence about human origins has reopened debates about a historical Adam across traditions.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/0/labe: What is a human being before God — and what went wrong?
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/0/text: Christians confess that humans are made in God’s image yet fallen into sin. But what is the image? Are we body and soul, or body, soul and spirit — or wholly physical? Where do souls come from? Do we inherit Adam’s guilt, or only his mortality? Can fallen humans choose God, and what kind of freedom do we have? And why did doctrines of human nature so often serve hierarchies of sex and race?
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/1/text: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness … male and female created he them”; “the LORD God formed man of the dust … and man became a living soul”; “your whole spirit and soul and body”.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/2/text: “In sin did my mother conceive me”; “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned”; “by nature the children of wrath”.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/3/text: Irenaeus distinguishes the image (human nature, including the body) from the likeness (the Spirit’s gift, lost and restored), and sees humanity as created young, to grow.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/4/labe: Tertullian: the soul and the guilt of Eve
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/4/text: Tertullian ties the soul’s origin to procreation and, in ascetic exhortation, addresses women as heirs of Eve’s guilt — words later central to feminist critiques.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/5/text: On the Soul teaches that souls are propagated with bodies, so that all were “in Adam”.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/6/text: Origen speculates that souls existed before bodies and fell to different degrees — a view later condemned.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/7/labe: Gregory of Nyssa: the image in freedom and in all humanity
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/7/text: On the Making of Man locates the image in freedom and reason and in humanity as a whole.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/8/labe: Chrysostom: Adam’s heirs inherit death, not guilt
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/8/text: The Antiochene reading of Romans 5 that became characteristic of the East.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/9/text: Pelagius and Caelestius hold that Adam harmed his descendants only by bad example and that humans can obey God’s commands.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/10/tex: Augustine teaches inherited guilt and corruption, transmitted through generation and marked by concupiscence.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/11/lab: Creationism of the soul (Jerome); Augustine undecided
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/11/tex: Jerome holds that God creates each soul; Augustine confesses he cannot decide between this and traducianism.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/12/tex: African bishops, backed by Pope Zosimus and the emperor, condemn the denial of original sin and of the need for grace.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/13/tex: Affirms that Adam’s sin passed both death and sin to all, and that even the beginning of faith is grace — while rejecting predestination to evil.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/14/lab: Constantinople II condemns pre-existence of souls (553)
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/14/tex: Anathemas associated with the council reject the Origenist teaching that souls pre-exist bodies.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/15/lab: Aquinas: the image in the rational mind
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/15/tex: Scholastic theology locates the image in intellect and will, present in all humans, renewed by grace.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/16/lab: Council of Vienne: the soul is the form of the body (1312)
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/16/tex: Defines that the rational soul is of itself the form of the human body — classical Catholic holistic dualism.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/17/tex: Erasmus argues that grace-aided free will can apply itself to salvation; behind him stands the patristic defence of free choice.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/18/lab: Luther: the bondage of the will
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/18/tex: Luther replies that the fallen will is a captive, ridden by God or Satan; the Reformed confessions teach total depravity.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/19/tex: Zwingli calls original sin a defect or disease rather than guilt, and doubts the damnation of believers’ infants.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/20/tex: Trent teaches that Adam’s sin is transmitted by propagation, that baptism truly removes its guilt, and that remaining concupiscence is not sin in the proper sense — against Reformation views.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/21/lab: Valladolid: are Indigenous Americans fully human image-bearers? (1550)
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/21/tex: Las Casas argues against Sepúlveda’s Aristotelian “natural slaves” that the peoples of the Americas are rational image-bearers with rights.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/22/lab: Flacius: sin is the substance of fallen humanity
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/22/tex: In debate with Strigel, Flacius pushes Luther’s language to say original sin is the very substance of fallen human nature.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/23/tex: Article I distinguishes human nature, which God still creates and Christ assumed, from original sin which corrupts it.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/24/tex: The Remonstrants and later Wesley affirm inability by nature but a universal grace that frees the will to respond.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/25/tex: Reformed covenant theology makes Adam the representative head whose guilt is imputed to all.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/26/lab: Edwards: freedom of the will and original sin
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/26/tex: Edwards argues for compatibilist freedom (1754) and that God constitutes humanity one with Adam (1758).
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/27/lab: Image of God and the slavery debates
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/27/tex: Pro-slavery theologians invoke the “curse of Ham” and household codes; abolitionists and enslaved preachers invoke the image of God and “one blood”.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/28/lab: Trichotomy: spirit, soul and body (Watchman Nee)
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/28/tex: Revived by Delitzsch and Keswick writers, popularised in China and worldwide by Nee’s The Spiritual Man.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/29/tex: Barth rejects capacity views and reads the image as encounter — humanity as male and female in covenant partnership.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/30/lab: Romanides: ancestral sin, not inherited guilt
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/30/tex: Orthodox theologians sharpen the Greek patristic view into a critique of Augustine.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/31/lab: Whose sin? Feminist and Black critiques
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/31/tex: Valerie Saiving argues that “sin as pride” reflects male experience; James Cone names racism as sin. Both question how the doctrine of sin was written, recalling Tertullian’s and Aquinas’ words about women.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/32/tex: Old Testament scholars read the image against ancient Near Eastern royal ideology: humans are God’s representatives and stewards.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/33/tex: Nancey Murphy and others argue for a non-reductive physicalist anthropology with hope in resurrection.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/34/tex: Genomic evidence that modern humans descend from a population of thousands, not two, prompts debates among evangelicals and Catholics: Adam as historical individual, as representative head of a population, or as archetype.
doctrines/humanity-sin/flow/nodes/35/tex: The Augustinian, federal and Eastern accounts of original sin coexist with Wesleyan and Zwinglian alternatives; relational and functional readings of the image now dominate scholarship; dualists and physicalists debate the soul; and Global South churches, often living with spiritual-power cosmologies and ethnic conflict, emphasise both the dignity of persons and the reality of sin’s bondage.
doctrines/revelation-apologetics/questio: How does God make himself known, and how should Christians give a reason for their faith?
doctrines/revelation-apologetics/summary: Christians agree that God has spoken supremely in Jesus Christ, but disagree over how much can be known of God from nature and reason, whether revelation has ended, and how faith should be defended — by proofs, evidence, presuppositions, a cumulative case, or not by argument at all.
doctrines/revelation-apologetics/longTex:
Scripture speaks of God’s witness in creation and conscience (Psalm 19; Romans 1-2; Acts 14 and 17) and of his final word in his Son (Hebrews 1). From these texts theologians developed the distinction between general and special revelation. The earliest apologists faced pagan philosophers and Roman magistrates: Justin Martyr saw “seeds of the Word” in Greek philosophy, while Tertullian asked what Athens had to do with Jerusalem; Origen answered Celsus point by point.

From the seventh century, the most demanding apologetic setting was Islam, which presented itself as the final revelation. Christians under Muslim rule wrote the first Christian theology in Arabic: John of Damascus polemically, Catholicos Timothy I courteously before the caliph al-Mahdi (782), Theodore Abu Qurrah with philosophical criteria for true religion. The kalām cosmological argument revived by modern apologists has its roots in this shared Islamic-Christian intellectual world. Later encounters — Ramon Llull, Nicholas of Cusa, Henry Martyn, Karl Pfander’s defeat at Agra (1854) — show the same mix of polemic and dialogue.

In the Latin West, Anselm’s “faith seeking understanding” and Aquinas’ five ways defined a classical natural theology, later made Catholic dogma at Vatican I (1870). Calvin spoke of a universal “sense of deity” distorted by sin. In the age of deism and science, Butler’s probabilistic Analogy and Paley’s watchmaker became staples of English apologetics, while Hume and later Darwin undermined their foundations. Pascal and Kierkegaard turned instead to the heart, the wager and the passionate leap of faith.

The 20th century saw Barth’s thunderous “No!” to Emil Brunner’s natural theology (1934), written in the shadow of Nazi ideology, alongside a flowering of Protestant apologetic schools: classical (Craig), evidential (Montgomery, Habermas), presuppositional (Van Til), cumulative-case (Mitchell, Swinburne) and Reformed epistemology (Plantinga, Wolterstorff). Meanwhile, claims of continuing revelation — from Montanist oracles and the Quaker Inner Light to Latter-day Saint scripture (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy) and Pentecostal prophecy — tested the historic conviction, shared by Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, that public revelation was completed in Christ.
doctrines/revelation-apologetics/flow/no: How does God make himself known — and can faith be rationally defended?

Is God known through nature, conscience and reason, or only through his self-revelation in Christ and Scripture? Has revelation ended, or does God still speak through prophets? And how should Christians defend their faith before philosophers, sceptics and other religions?
“The heavens declare the glory of God”; “he left not himself without witness”; “the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen … so that they are without excuse”.
Hebrews 1:1-2; John 1:18; Jude 3; 1 Peter 3:15

“God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake … hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son”; “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints”; “be ready always to give an answer … a reason of the hope that is in you”.
Justin Martyr: seeds of the Word in philosophy
The first great apologist sees the Logos sowing truth among the Greeks.
Tertullian: Athens and Jerusalem
Tertullian’s rhetoric sets faith over against philosophy — though he himself used philosophy freely.
Origen’s Against Celsus
The fullest early apology answers a learned pagan critic point by point, from miracles to the resurrection.
General and special revelation: God’s two books
The Fathers, especially Augustine, speak of the book of creation alongside the book of Scripture.
The rise of Islam: a rival claim to final revelation
Islam’s claim that the Qur’an completes and corrects earlier scriptures creates a new apologetic setting for Christians living under Muslim rule.
John of Damascus on the “heresy of the Ishmaelites”
Writing under the Umayyads, John treats Islam as a Christian heresy in a sharply polemical chapter.
Timothy I’s dialogue with Caliph al-Mahdi
The Church of the East’s patriarch defends the Trinity courteously before the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad.
Arabic Christian apologetics (Abu Qurrah and others)
Melkite, Syriac Orthodox and East Syriac theologians write in Arabic, using kalām methods to defend the Trinity and the Bible.
Anselm’s ontological argument: faith seeking understanding
God is that than which nothing greater can be thought; such a being must exist.
Aquinas: the five ways and the preambles of faith
Aquinas rejects the ontological argument but proves God from effects, distinguishing truths reason can reach from mysteries of faith.
Calvin: the sense of deity and the spectacles of Scripture
All people have a seed of religion, but sin distorts it; Scripture acts as spectacles to see God rightly.
Public revelation closed (Westminster; later Dei Verbum)
Westminster declares the “former ways” of revelation “now ceased”; Catholic teaching likewise expects no new public revelation.
Pascal: the wager and the heart
Pascal’s Pensées turn from proofs to the human condition and the practical wager.
Butler and the evidences: probability as guide
Against the deists, Butler argues by analogy and probability; evidential apologetics follows.
Hume’s critique of design and miracles
Hume’s Dialogues and essay on miracles become the classic sceptical objections.
Paley’s Natural Theology: the watchmaker
Paley answers with the most famous design argument, soon to be challenged by Darwin.
Continuing revelation: new prophets and scriptures
From Montanus to the Quakers’ Inner Light, Joseph Smith’s Book of Mormon (1830, outside historic Nicene orthodoxy) and Pentecostal prophecy, some claim God still reveals.
Kierkegaard: faith as passionate leap
Kierkegaard attacks rational Christianity: faith appropriates the absolute paradox.
Agra debate (1854): biblical criticism turned against missionaries
Rahmatullah Kairanawi uses European higher criticism against Pfander, reshaping Muslim–Christian polemics in South Asia.
Vatican I: God knowable by natural reason (1870)
Dei Filius defines natural knowledge of God and condemns both rationalism and fideism.
Barmen: Jesus Christ the one Word of God (1934)
The Confessing Church rejects any other source of revelation alongside Christ.
Brunner: a point of contact
Brunner’s Nature and Grace defends a formal image and limited natural revelation.
Barth’s Nein!
Barth rejects all natural theology as the root of the church’s capitulation to ideology.
C. S. Lewis: moral argument and trilemma
Mere Christianity popularises the moral argument and the “mad, bad or God” trilemma.
Van Til: presuppositional apologetics
No neutral ground: only the triune God makes reason intelligible.
Dei Verbum (1965): revelation complete in Christ
Vatican II presents revelation as God’s personal self-communication, complete in Christ, transmitted in Scripture and Tradition.
Classical apologetics revived: the kalām argument
William Lane Craig revives the medieval Islamic kalām argument within a two-step classical method.
Cumulative case: Swinburne and Mitchell
Theism defended as the best overall explanation, by converging probabilities.
Reformed epistemology: belief in God as properly basic
Plantinga and Wolterstorff argue belief in God can be rational without arguments.
Today: apologetics in a plural world

Natural theology has revived in analytic philosophy; online debate culture popularises classical, evidential and presuppositional methods; Barthian theology remains sceptical; and in Africa, Asia and the Middle East apologetics often concerns Islam, traditional religion, prosperity teaching and claims of new prophets more than Western secularism.
